newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine has no regrets over Lebed sacking.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine has no regrets over Lebed sacking.

text.p: Ukraine is likely to have few regrets over the dismissal of Russian security chief Alexander Lebed who annoyed the former Soviet republic by reviving doubts about its control of the Black Sea port of Sevastopol.

"Lebed's comments about Russia's status regarding Sevastopol was an unfriendly act and tantamount to interference in Ukraine's affairs," Interfax Ukraine news agency quoted Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko as saying on Friday.
Udovenko was referring to comments made by Lebed last month.

"Ukraine is concerned that there are constant doubts being raised in Russia about Ukrainian sovereignty and independence," Udovenko told a meeting in Moscow of senior leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Sevastopol is located in Ukraine's Crimea peninsula and is the headquarters of the Fleet, still disputed by Ukraine and Russia five years after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The outspoken Lebed was sacked as head of Russia's Security Council on Thursday by President Boris Yeltsin, who accused him of harbouring ambitions to become president and failing to work with other players on his team.
Lebed was one of a number of Russian politicians who have sought to prove their nationalist credentials by reviving claims that the Sevastopol base was Russian territory.
Russia's State Duma lower house of parliament in 1993 first openly staked such a claim, which was quickly disavowed by Yeltsin and other Kremlin leaders.
The Duma this week urged the Kremlin to halt the long process of splitting the Black Sea Fleet, a move denounced by the Ukrainian parliament on Friday.

Interfax quoted a parliamentary resolution as saying that if Russia acted on the Duma proposal to halt the division of the Fleet, it would demand the immediate removal of Russian forces from Ukrainian territory.
"Ukraine considers the Duma's actions as an encroachment on Ukraine's sovereignty amounting to a territorial claim on Ukraine," it said.

But the agency said Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, also in Moscow for the CIS meeting, had received assurances from Russian counterpart Viktor Chernomyrdin that the Kremlin viewed Crimea and Sevastopol as Ukraine's territory.

Chernomyrdin was quoted by Russia's Itar-Tass agency as saying that the two sides could reach final agreement on the Fleet next month. The Fleet is considered the main sticking point preventing the two sides signing a friendship treaty.
Ukraine firmly backed Yeltsin's successful re-election bid against Communist Gennady Zyuganov in July.
